drills.los_text: discuss the different types of individual wealth and how wealth is created and distributed globally
drills.reading_name: An Overview of Private Wealth Management

questions.stem: How individual wealth is created most likely matters because:

options.A: The source of wealth shapes concentration, liquidity, and the planning agenda.
options.B: Inherited and entrepreneurial wealth produce identical balance sheets.
options.C: Only the current market value of financial capital affects the plan.

rationales.A: Entrepreneurship tends to produce concentrated and illiquid holdings; employment and executive awards often mean concentrated employer stock; inheritance brings multi-generational governance and estate issues. The source shapes concentration, liquidity, and the planning agenda more than the dollar amount alone does.
rationales.B: The two sources typically imply very different liquidity and governance needs, so they do not produce identical balance sheets and source-of-wealth questions cannot be skipped once net worth is known.
rationales.C: Source drives concentration, liquidity, and planning even when two clients have the same net worth, so it is not a biographical detail: it changes IPS constraints and estate planning.

questions.curriculum_ref: PWM LOS a — sources of wealth

questions.stem: Wealth from sale of a founder’s operating company is most likely to present as:

options.A: A tax-deferred defined-benefit pension.
options.B: A ladder of liquid public securities with no single-name risk.
options.C: Concentrated, often illiquid exposure tied to one business.

rationales.A: A defined-benefit pension is employment-style wealth, not sale-of-business wealth, and it would reduce the problem to required-return arithmetic on a spend-down portfolio, which is not what founder wealth presents.
rationales.B: Founder wealth is typically the opposite of a diversified public book: single-name risk and illiquidity are its defining features, which is exactly why diversification and liquidity events are planning priorities.
rationales.C: Entrepreneurial wealth is concentrated and illiquid, tied to one business, so diversification, liquidity events, and succession and estate planning dominate the agenda. That source, not just the headline net worth, sets the work.

questions.stem: Private-client segments, moving toward more customized advice, are most likely ordered:

options.A: Mass affluent, UHNW, mass market, HNW.
options.B: UHNW, HNW, mass affluent, mass market.
options.C: Mass market, mass affluent, HNW, UHNW.

rationales.A: This sequence is not ordered by wealth at all — it jumps from mass affluent to UHNW and back down to mass market. It treats the segments as an unordered set of marketing labels rather than the ladder of advice intensity being tested.
rationales.B: The order is reversed. Customization rises with wealth rather than falling: the largest pools receive the most bespoke advice, not standardized products only.
rationales.C: The ladder runs mass market, then mass affluent, then high-net-worth (HNW), then ultra-high-net-worth (UHNW). Standardized products sit at the base, while family-office service, philanthropy, and complex estate and direct-deal work sit at the UHNW apex.

questions.stem: The global distribution of individual wealth is most accurately described as:

options.A: Concentrated in a few developed markets, with a now-flat global pyramid.
options.B: A steep pyramid with a broad base and a narrow apex, uneven across regions.
options.C: Roughly uniform across households within each region.

rationales.A: Emerging-market wealth creation changes where the apex sits, but it does not make the pyramid disappear; concentration remains a planning fact rather than a historical one.
rationales.B: Global individual wealth is a steep pyramid: a broad mass-market base and a narrow HNW/UHNW apex that holds a disproportionate share. The pattern is regionally uneven and still shifting as emerging-market wealth is created.
rationales.C: The distribution is highly unequal rather than uniform within a region, which is why segment and source of wealth matter and why advice is not standardized globally above some minimum account size.

questions.stem: The private wealth management process is most likely sequenced as:

options.A: Discovery, IPS, implementation, then monitoring and review.
options.B: IPS, implementation, monitoring, with discovery only if the client objects.
options.C: Implementation, then discovery, then IPS and monitoring.

rationales.A: The process is a repeatable cycle: discovery of goals, circumstances, risk tolerance, and constraints; then the IPS; then implementation through asset allocation, tax-aware construction, and choice of vehicles; then monitoring and review as life and markets change. Much of the value is planning, coaching, and tax and estate coordination, not only security selection.
rationales.B: The IPS is the output of discovery, not a substitute for it, so it cannot be published first with discovery treated as optional detail the client has to ask for.
rationales.C: Discovery precedes the IPS and implementation. Goals are not reverse-engineered from holdings: you do not buy the portfolio first and interview later.

questions.stem: For a senior executive whose wealth comes from salary, bonus, and equity awards, the planning issue arising first is most likely:

options.A: Concentration in employer stock and options.
options.B: Multi-generational family-office governance.
options.C: A perpetual, tax-exempt institutional horizon.

rationales.A: Employment and executive wealth typically accumulates as concentrated employer equity plus option positions, so the first planning issues are single-name concentration risk and the tax timing of vesting and exercise. That is a different source problem from the entrepreneur's illiquid private operating company or the inheritor's stewardship agenda, and it drives hedging, staged diversification, and exercise sequencing before any other agenda item.
rationales.B: Multi-generational family-office governance is a pattern of ultra-high-net-worth and inherited wealth, where several generations and an existing family entity create a genuine governance need. It is not the automatic first issue for an executive who has no operating company and no heirs, and treating it as the default agenda for every high-net-worth client misreads where the wealth came from.
rationales.C: Executives are taxable private clients with finite, life-cycle horizons and sole decision authority, so their constraints are the reverse of an endowment's. Vesting restricted stock does not convert the portfolio into a perpetual, tax-exempt pool run by an investment committee; taxes and a definite horizon remain binding.

drills.los_text: evaluate how changes in human capital, financial capital, and economic net worth across the financial stages of an individual's life influence their financial decision making
drills.reading_name: An Overview of Private Wealth Management

questions.stem: Human capital is most likely:

options.A: The current market value of the client's investment portfolio.
options.B: The present value of expected future labor income.
options.C: A qualitative endowment of education and credentials.

rationales.A: The current market value of assets already accumulated and available to invest is financial capital, the other half of the economic balance sheet, not human capital.
rationales.B: Human capital is the present value of expected future labor income — wages, salaries, and self-employment earnings — discounted at a rate appropriate to the risk and stability of that income stream. It is typically the largest asset of a young individual and declines as retirement approaches. It is treated as a non-tradeable asset whose risk profile depends on the career: bond-like for stable professions, equity-like for cyclical or entrepreneurial ones.
rationales.C: Education and credentials are inputs to earning power, but human capital is quantified rather than left qualitative: it is the discounted present value of the future labor income those credentials are expected to produce.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old professional earns a salary of $150,000, expects salary growth of 3% per year, and retires at age 65 after 35 earning years. At a 6% discount rate, the present value of human capital is closest to:

rationales.A: $5,250,000 is 35 × $150,000, the simple sum of 35 years of salary at today's level with no discounting applied. Ignoring the 6% discount rate overstates human capital by roughly $2.1 million here.
rationales.B: Use the growing-annuity formula: HC = W₀/(r−g) × [1 − ((1+g)/(1+r))^n] = 150,000/(0.06−0.03) × [1 − (1.03/1.06)^35] = 5,000,000 × [1 − 0.3661] = 5,000,000 × 0.6339 ≈ $3,170,000, or about $3.17 million. The 3% growth rate raises each future salary while the 6% discount rate reduces it, and the net 3% spread drives the multiple applied to the current $150,000.
rationales.C: $150,000 is a single year's salary — the first cash flow in the stream rather than the present value of all 35 years of it.

questions.stem: Financial capital is most likely:

options.A: The present value of expected future labor income.
options.B: The current market value of all investable assets.
options.C: The taxable brokerage portfolio and cash reserves only.

rationales.A: The present value of expected future labor income, discounted at a rate reflecting the risk of that income, is human capital, not financial capital.
rationales.B: Financial capital is the current market value of all tradeable and non-tradeable investable assets: taxable brokerage accounts, retirement accounts, real estate equity, business ownership stakes, and cash reserves. It excludes human capital, which is future labor income, and excludes non-investable assets such as personal possessions. It forms the balance sheet from which portfolio decisions are made.
rationales.C: Financial capital spans all investable assets at current market value. Retirement accounts and non-tradeable holdings such as real estate equity and private business stakes belong inside it, so counting only the taxable brokerage portfolio and cash understates it.

questions.stem: Net wealth is most likely:

options.A: Human capital plus financial capital, net of liabilities and future consumption.
options.B: Financial capital net of liabilities, with human capital excluded.
options.C: Financial capital alone.

rationales.A: Net wealth, or economic net worth, equals human capital + financial capital − liabilities (mortgages and other debts) − the present value of future consumption liabilities. It gives a more complete picture than financial-capital-only accounting because it captures both the earning potential embedded in human capital and the future consumption obligations that earning potential must fund, and it is the framework for life-cycle planning and portfolio structure.
rationales.B: Human capital belongs on the economic balance sheet even though it is not tradeable, and the present value of future consumption belongs there as a liability. Netting liabilities against financial capital alone leaves out both.
rationales.C: Financial capital alone is the market value of investable assets. Net wealth adds human capital to it and then deducts liabilities and the present value of future consumption obligations.

questions.stem: For a 25-year-old adult, human capital and financial capital are most likely:

options.A: Equal to each other and constant over the life cycle.
options.B: Small human capital and large financial capital.
options.C: Large human capital and small financial capital.

rationales.A: This denies the compositional shift that defines the life cycle. Total capital is relatively stable, but human capital declines while financial capital grows, so the two are neither equal nor constant.
rationales.B: This reverses the life-cycle pattern. Savings have barely begun at 25, so financial capital is small, while decades of future earnings make human capital large.
rationales.C: At age 25 human capital is large, representing decades of future earnings, while financial capital is small. By middle age, around 45, human capital has declined as fewer earning years remain and financial capital has grown through saving. At retirement, around 65, human capital is near zero apart from social security or pension entitlements and financial capital finances the remaining years. Total capital is relatively stable, but its composition shifts dramatically, which is what informs the equity-versus-bond allocation across the life cycle.

questions.stem: When a client's human capital is bond-like, the allocation of financial capital is most likely:

options.A: Tilted further toward fixed income.
options.B: Tilted toward equity.
options.C: Set without reference to human capital.

rationales.A: Stable earnings already act like a large bond holding on the total-wealth balance sheet, so adding a fixed-income tilt in the financial portfolio compounds the same exposure rather than balancing it.
rationales.B: When human capital is bond-like — the stable earnings of a tenured professor or government employee — it effectively acts as a large fixed-income holding. Balancing the total portfolio therefore argues for a higher equity allocation within financial capital, and an allocation as aggressive as 100% equity in financial capital can be reasonable when bond-like human capital is large relative to it. The reverse holds for equity-like human capital.
rationales.C: Human capital is the dominant asset of the total-wealth balance sheet early in a career, so its character does carry an implication: bond-like human capital supports a heavier equity tilt in financial capital. Setting the allocation from financial capital alone ignores that.

questions.stem: When a client's human capital is equity-like, the allocation of financial capital is most likely:

options.A: Set without reference to human capital.
options.B: Tilted further toward equity.
options.C: Tilted toward fixed income.

rationales.A: The character of human capital does carry an implication. When earnings move with markets — banker bonuses, founder equity, sales commissions — the balancing response in financial capital is a tilt toward fixed income, so the allocation cannot be set from financial capital alone.
rationales.B: Market-correlated earnings already supply equity-like exposure on the total-wealth balance sheet. Adding more equity in the financial portfolio concentrates the risk instead of offsetting it, leaving equity earnings on top of an equity portfolio.
rationales.C: When human capital is equity-like — bonuses correlated with the market, as for an investment banker, a technology founder, or a commissioned salesperson — earnings volatility resembles equity risk. Financial capital should therefore be tilted toward fixed income to balance that equity-like earnings exposure. Ignoring the nature of human capital leads to concentrated risk, with equity-like earnings sitting alongside an equity portfolio.

questions.stem: A client's human capital is most likely:

options.A: Unaffected by disability.
options.B: Transferred to heirs at death.
options.C: Extinguished by death or disability.

rationales.A: This overlooks morbidity risk. Disability reduces or eliminates the ability to work and therefore the human capital that depends on it, which is precisely the case for disability insurance.
rationales.B: Human capital is non-tradeable and is extinguished at death rather than passing to heirs the way financial assets do. That is why life insurance is needed to replace it for dependents.
rationales.C: Human capital exists only while the person is alive and earning. Early death eliminates it and premature disability eliminates or reduces it. This creates mortality and morbidity risk, hedged with life insurance to replace the human capital lost to dependents on death and with disability insurance to replace the human capital lost to an inability to work.

questions.stem: The life insurance need of a client with dependents is most likely based on:

options.A: A fixed multiple of current salary.
options.B: The present value of human capital lost to dependents.
options.C: The client's current expenses alone.

rationales.A: A fixed multiple such as ten times salary is a rule of thumb that ignores existing assets, the number and ages of dependents, and remaining career length. The need is anchored instead to the present value of human capital lost to dependents, net of financial capital and the surviving spouse's own earning power.
rationales.B: The life insurance need is broadly the amount required to replace the present value of the human capital that dependents lose on the insured's death. More precisely, it is the present value of future needs — spouse living expenses, children's costs, education — less financial capital already accumulated, less the present value of the surviving spouse's own labor income, with adjustments for social security survivor benefits and insurance already in force. The need typically declines with age as human capital falls and financial capital accumulates.
rationales.C: Current expenses are only one input to the present value of future needs. Human capital is the anchor, because the death benefit replaces the future earnings dependents lose, measured net of financial capital and the survivor's own income.

questions.stem: A client's human capital has a present value of $2 million, the family's present value of expected consumption is $2.5 million, existing financial capital is $500,000, and the present value of the spouse's expected earnings is $700,000. Using the needs-analysis approach, the life insurance need is closest to:

rationales.A: The $2,000,000 figure is the client's own human capital present value, used as though the entire future income stream had to be insured. The needs-analysis approach does not start from human capital; it starts from the family's present value of expected consumption, $2,500,000, and then subtracts the resources the family already has. Taking human capital as the answer ignores both the $500,000 of existing financial capital and the $700,000 present value of the spouse's expected earnings, so it neither answers the question asked nor nets the available offsets.
rationales.B: Need = present value of family consumption − existing financial capital − present value of the surviving spouse's earnings = 2,500,000 − 500,000 − 700,000 = 1,300,000. The needs-analysis approach measures the additional capital that would have to be in place at the earner's death to fund the family's remaining consumption, after the assets already owned and the income the surviving spouse will continue to earn have done their part. The client's own $2,000,000 of human capital does not enter the calculation: it is the resource that disappears, and insurance replaces only the part of it the family still needs.
rationales.C: $5,700,000 is the sum of every figure in the problem — 2,000,000 + 2,500,000 + 500,000 + 700,000 — rather than the consumption need net of available resources. Existing financial capital and the spouse's expected earnings reduce the insurance need; adding them to it, along with the client's own human capital, overstates the $1,300,000 requirement more than fourfold.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old primary earner wants to hedge the loss of human capital over the remaining earning years. The most appropriate vehicle is most likely:

options.A: term life insurance.
options.B: either, since purpose does not guide the choice.
options.C: whole life insurance.

rationales.A: Term life insurance provides a pure death benefit at low cost for a stated period, so a 20- to 30-year term can be matched to the years over which human capital is being converted into earnings. That is precisely the exposure being hedged: the risk that the earner dies before the income stream has been realized. Whole or permanent life also pays a death benefit, but it bundles a cash-value savings element that raises the premium for a given amount of coverage, and it is generally bought for estate-planning purposes rather than for replacing lost earnings. A blend of the two can be appropriate where both needs exist.
rationales.B: Vehicle selection sits squarely within the private-wealth advisor's remit, and a clear framework governs it: match the product to the purpose. Term coverage replaces human capital during the working years; permanent coverage serves estate objectives and liquidity at death. Saying that nothing guides the choice ignores both the cost difference between the two vehicles and the finite horizon over which human capital needs hedging.
rationales.C: Whole life suits permanent needs — estate liquidity, a legacy objective, coverage that must be in force whenever death occurs — and its cash value makes it an expensive way to buy a given death benefit. For hedging human capital it is dominated by term, whose low-cost pure death benefit can be sized to the earning years and allowed to lapse once human capital has been converted into financial capital. Permanent coverage therefore does not dominate term in every circumstance.

questions.stem: Under the total portfolio perspective, a private client's asset allocation is most appropriately set by considering:

options.A: financial capital only.
options.B: both, but with the financial allocation independent of human capital's risk.
options.C: human capital and financial capital together.

rationales.A: Human capital is not tradeable, but that is not a reason to leave it off the client's balance sheet. For a young professional it is usually the largest single asset, and excluding it defeats the purpose of the total portfolio perspective, which is precisely that human capital and financial capital be considered together when the financial allocation is set.
rationales.B: This keeps human capital on the balance sheet but refuses to let its character influence the financial mix, which discards the practical content of the perspective. Whether human capital is bond-like (stable, secure earnings) or equity-like (variable, cyclical, firm-specific) determines how much equity risk the financial portfolio can carry before total-wealth risk exceeds what the client wants. The financial allocation should be set to offset the human capital exposure, not independently of it.
rationales.C: The total portfolio includes human capital and financial capital together, and the allocation of financial assets is set in light of the risk and return properties of human capital. Where human capital is fixed-income-like, the financial portfolio can carry more equity; where it is equity-like, the financial portfolio should hold more fixed income. A young professional with a stable career and $50,000 of financial capital may reasonably hold 100% equity in that financial capital, because the dominant exposure in total wealth is the bond-like human capital. Ignoring human capital leads to a financial allocation that is suboptimal relative to the client's desired total risk profile, which is why this perspective is central to lifecycle allocation.

questions.stem: A client earns $150,000 a year, income is expected to grow 3% annually over an essentially perpetual career, and the appropriate discount rate is 6%. Using the growing-perpetuity approximation, the present value of human capital is closest to:

rationales.A: $2,500,000 is 150,000/0.06, the level perpetuity W/r. It discounts the income stream correctly but treats it as flat, dropping the 3% growth entirely and so understating the growing perpetuity W/(r − g).
rationales.B: For a very long career, where n is large and (1 + g)/(1 + r) < 1, the finite growing-annuity formula converges on the growing perpetuity, so human capital ≈ W₀/(r − g) = 150,000/(0.06 − 0.03) = $5,000,000. The approximation gives a quick estimate when precision on the distant tail of the income stream matters little, and it serves as a convenient upper bound: because a real career ends, the perpetuity overstates finite-career human capital by the value of the tail beyond retirement.
rationales.C: $1,670,000 is 150,000/0.09, which adds the growth rate to the discount rate as W/(r + g) instead of subtracting it. Growth raises the present value of an income stream and so must reduce the denominator; adding it instead triples the effective discount and understates human capital by more than $3 million.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old primary earner has human capital with a present value of $2.5 million, a family present value of consumption of $2 million, financial capital of $400,000, spouse human capital of $600,000, and $500,000 of life insurance in force. Using the needs-analysis approach, the additional insurance need is closest to:

rationales.A: Consumption need of $2,000,000 less financial capital of $400,000, less the $600,000 present value of the spouse's human capital, less the $500,000 of coverage already in force leaves $500,000 of additional insurance required to replace the primary earner's contribution in full. Each subtraction is a resource the family can already draw on, so only the residual has to be bought. The earner's own $2,500,000 of human capital is not the target amount; it is the asset at risk, and the needs-analysis approach asks only how much of the family's consumption that asset was funding.
rationales.B: $2,000,000 is the family's present value of expected consumption taken as the answer before any offset. It credits neither the $400,000 of financial capital, nor the $600,000 present value of the spouse's earnings, nor the $500,000 of in-force coverage, and so overstates the additional requirement fourfold.
rationales.C: $2,500,000 is the full present value of the earner's human capital, with no offsets for existing financial capital, the spouse's earnings, or coverage already in place. The needs-analysis approach begins with the family's consumption need rather than with human capital, and then nets available resources against it.

questions.stem: Over a client's earning career, the life insurance need typically declines most likely because:

options.A: human capital falls as fewer earning years remain.
options.B: financial capital is depleted with age.
options.C: human capital rises as peak earnings arrive later.

rationales.A: As a person ages the present value of human capital declines, because fewer earning years remain to be discounted, while financial capital grows as savings accumulate. At the same time dependents are raised and become self-supporting and mortgages are paid down. Together these forces reduce the amount of capital required to protect dependents against the loss of the earner's income, which is why both the insurance need and the insurance actually held typically decline across the earning career: the need follows the human capital lifecycle.
rationales.B: Financial capital normally accumulates rather than depletes during the earning years, as income exceeds consumption and savings compound; depletion belongs to the retirement phase, after human capital has already run down. The direction of the effect is also wrong: more financial capital on hand means less of the family's consumption has to be funded by an insurance payout, which lowers the need rather than raising it.
rationales.C: Human capital falls with age rather than rising. Even where the wage path peaks in mid-career, the present value of remaining earnings shrinks because fewer years of income are left to discount, and that shrinking human capital is exactly what makes the insurance need decline.

questions.stem: The role of disability insurance in a private client's risk plan is most likely that it:

options.A: protects dependents against loss of human capital at the insured's death.
options.B: protects against loss of human capital from an inability to work while living.
options.C: is redundant once adequate life insurance is in place.

rationales.A: Protecting dependents against the loss of human capital at death is the function of life insurance. Disability coverage addresses a different contingency, in which the insured survives but cannot work, so the income stops while the household's consumption — including the disabled earner's own expenses — continues.
rationales.B: Disability insurance protects against the loss of human capital caused by an inability to work while still living. For most ages during the working career the probability of a disabling illness or injury exceeds the probability of death, so this is the larger of the two risks. Without coverage, an extended disability drives human capital to zero while the household depletes financial capital to fund consumption, and the disabled earner's own expenses continue as well. Typical policies replace 50% to 70% of income, and the coverage adds to rather than replaces life insurance.
rationales.C: Life insurance pays only on death and so leaves morbidity risk entirely uncovered. Because disability is the more likely event during the working years, and because household expenses continue through it, adequate life insurance does nothing to make disability coverage unnecessary; the two hedge distinct risks to the same human capital.

questions.stem: In valuing the human capital of a client whose career income is volatile, career risk is most appropriately reflected by:

options.A: a discount rate that rises with the risk of the income stream.
options.B: a lower income growth rate, with the discount rate unchanged.
options.C: no adjustment, since one standard discount rate applies to every stream.

rationales.A: The discount rate applied to an income stream should reflect that stream's risk. Low-risk earnings — a tenured post, secure public-sector employment — warrant a rate close to the risk-free rate plus a small margin. High-risk earnings — commissioned sales, a technology start-up, entertainment — warrant a higher rate that reflects the volatility of the income. Human capital calculations left unadjusted overstate present value for volatile careers, and so understate how much bond-like ballast the financial portfolio needs to carry.
rationales.B: The growth rate g represents expected wage growth, which is an estimate of the level of future income rather than of its uncertainty. Lowering g to stand in for career risk conflates the two and would still value two streams of identical expected growth but very different risk at the same rate. The adjustment belongs in the discount rate: riskier income streams take higher rates and produce lower human capital present values.
rationales.C: A single standard rate applied to every client would value the tenured professor's earnings and the commissioned salesperson's earnings alike, even though one stream is near-certain and the other is highly volatile. Reflecting the risk of the underlying career is exactly what the discount rate is there to do.

drills.los_text: justify how returns, risks, objectives, and constraints for individuals relate to their human and financial capital

questions.stem: Two 40-year-olds hold similar financial assets; one is a tenured civil servant and the other is a commission salesperson in a cyclical industry. A larger equity allocation in the financial portfolio is most appropriate for:

options.A: neither client.
options.B: the salesperson.
options.C: the civil servant.

rationales.A: The risk character of human capital is exactly what justifies a different portfolio tilt for the two clients. Two people of the same age with the same financial assets can warrant different financial-portfolio mixes, because total wealth is human capital plus financial capital and the risks of the two components combine.
rationales.B: Cyclical, commission-based income is equity-like human capital. Matching it with more equity in the financial portfolio concentrates total-wealth risk rather than balancing it: labor income and investment returns would fall together in a downturn, exactly when the client can least afford it. The salesperson's case argues for more fixed income in the financial portfolio, not more equity.
rationales.C: Stable, secure earnings behave like a large bond holding, so the civil servant's total wealth is already dominated by a bond-like asset and the financial portfolio can take more equity risk without pushing total-wealth risk too high. The salesperson's cyclical commission income is equity-like human capital and argues instead for more bonds in the financial portfolio to balance it.

questions.curriculum_ref: PWM LOS c — bond-like vs equity-like HC

questions.stem: A founder’s human capital is equity-like (variable, firm-specific). Relative to a tenured professor of the same age and financial wealth, the founder’s financial portfolio should most likely hold:

options.A: more bonds.
options.B: the same mix as the professor's.
options.C: more public equity.

rationales.A: Equity-like human capital calls for more bonds, or at least less equity beta, in the financial portfolio. The founder's total wealth already contains a concentrated, firm-specific, equity-like claim in the form of labor and business income, so filling the liquid portfolio with the same kind of risk would leave total-wealth risk almost entirely equity-like. Fixed income in the financial book offsets that exposure and supplies liquidity precisely when the business is under strain.
rationales.B: Age and the size of financial capital are not a complete risk story. The professor's tenured earnings are bond-like and the founder's are equity-like, and because the financial allocation is set in light of total wealth, that difference alone should move the two mixes apart even when age and financial capital match.
rationales.C: Adding public equity stacks a second equity-like exposure on top of the founder's already concentrated business income, concentrating total wealth rather than diversifying it. Entrepreneurial human capital is not a substitute for a diversified stock allocation — it is undiversified, illiquid and firm-specific — and levering the liquid book into the same risk compounds the problem.

questions.curriculum_ref: PWM LOS c — founder HC tilt

questions.stem: Target total-wealth equity is 30%. Human capital is bond-like (contributes no equity). Early career: HC 700,000, FC 300,000. Near retirement: HC 300,000, FC 700,000. Financial-portfolio equity weights are most likely:

options.A: 100% then about 43%.

rationales.A: The financial portfolio must supply whatever equity exposure human capital does not: w(equity in FC) = (target equity% × total wealth − equity contributed by HC) / FC. Early career, total wealth is 1,000,000, so target equity is 300,000; bond-like human capital contributes none of it, so the whole 300,000 has to come from a 300,000 financial portfolio — a 100% equity weight. Near retirement, total wealth is still 1,000,000 and target equity is still 300,000, but the financial portfolio has grown to 700,000, so the weight falls to 300,000/700,000 ≈ 43%. Holding total-wealth risk constant while bond-like human capital is spent down is the theoretical basis for a declining-equity glide path.
rationales.B: Thirty percent in both periods copies the total-wealth target straight into the financial portfolio, which would only be right if human capital already held the target mix. Because bond-like human capital contributes no equity, the financial book has to overweight equity to bring total wealth to 30%, so the financial-portfolio weight is not the total-wealth weight. Ignoring human capital in the calculation is the error: early career the correct weight is 100%, not 30%.
rationales.C: That path is backwards. Young, bond-like human capital implies a high financial-portfolio equity weight that declines as human capital is spent, not a conservative start that levers up later. Treating the shrinking human-capital stock as equity reverses the sign of the adjustment — if human capital were equity-like, the financial portfolio would hold less equity while human capital is large, not more.

questions.curriculum_ref: PWM LOS c — total-wealth glide path

questions.stem: Human-capital risks the investment portfolio cannot hedge, and their usual hedges, are most likely:

options.A: Life insurance for death, annuities for longevity, disability cover for earnings risk.
options.B: Annuities for death, term life expiring at retirement for longevity.
options.C: Higher equity for death, concentrated stock for longevity.

rationales.A: Portfolio beta does not replace the earner, so these risks are transferred through insurance products rather than managed in the asset allocation. Premature death destroys remaining human capital, so it is covered with life insurance sized to human capital at risk net of existing assets and existing coverage. Longevity is the opposite exposure — outliving the assets — and is hedged with annuities, which convert capital into lifetime income. Earnings and health risk are hedged with disability and health insurance, which protect the ability to keep converting human capital into earnings.
rationales.B: The two hedges are reversed. An annuity bought at age 30 pays income to someone who lives a long time; it does nothing for a family that loses the earner's remaining human capital. Term life that expires at retirement covers exactly the years in which the death-of-human-capital problem is already shrinking, and it lapses just as longevity risk begins, so neither risk is matched to its instrument.
rationales.C: Raising the equity weight or concentrating in a single stock hedges neither risk; it layers market risk on top of human-capital risk. The estate does not reliably grow faster in the state of the world that matters, an early death, and a concentrated position makes the survivors' wealth more dependent on outcomes they cannot control. Death and longevity are not diversifiable within the investment portfolio and have to be transferred through insurance and annuities.

questions.stem: Ability to take risk is high (long horizon, ample wealth vs needs, stable HC) but the client’s stated willingness is low. The adviser should most likely:

options.A: Follow willingness only when it exceeds ability.
options.B: Document both and generally follow the lower of the two.
options.C: Follow ability and disregard willingness.

rationales.A: Following willingness only when it is the higher of the two is a one-sided rule that systematically overrides low willingness, which is the opposite of the usual resolution. Applied here it would impose the high ability-based risk budget, so the portfolio would always carry more risk than the client prefers — the condition most likely to end in the plan being abandoned during a drawdown.
rationales.B: Where ability and willingness conflict, the adviser documents both in the IPS and generally implements the lower of the two while educating the client about the trade-off between the risk declined and the goals it would have funded. Here ability is high — long horizon, wealth ample relative to needs, stable human capital — but stated willingness is low, so willingness is the operative constraint. That is how individual constraints attach to the human-capital and financial-capital framework: coaching toward a higher budget over time is legitimate, forcing it is not.
rationales.C: Willingness to take risk is part of the risk objective for an individual, not an attitude to be discarded. Ability rests on objective measures — horizon, wealth relative to needs, the stability of human capital — but the IPS still has to be one the client will hold through a loss, so stated willingness is documented and respected rather than overridden.

questions.stem: Human capital is about 1,456,000. Survivors already have 300,000 of earmarked liquid assets and a 200,000 group life policy. Additional life-insurance need is most likely:

rationales.A: Additional need ≈ human capital at risk − assets and coverage already available to survivors: 1,456,000 − 300,000 of earmarked liquid assets − 200,000 of group life = 956,000. Resources the survivors already hold reduce the amount of new cover required. The constraint also shrinks over the life cycle: as the earner ages, remaining human capital falls and financial capital accumulates, so the insurance need declines with age.
rationales.B: Insuring the full 1,456,000 double-counts resources that would already support the survivors. Both the 300,000 of earmarked liquid assets and the 200,000 group policy are available to replace lost earnings, so in the human-capital approach both are netted against human capital, leaving an additional need of 956,000 rather than the gross figure.
rationales.C: Counting only the 200,000 group policy ignores the earmarked financial assets, which are subtracted as well. Assets dedicated to survivors do not stop counting because they sit in the investment portfolio: the human-capital approach nets both existing coverage and earmarked assets, giving 1,456,000 − 300,000 − 200,000 = 956,000.

drills.los_text: evaluate how various types of taxes imposed on individual investors and the impact of inflation influence investment decisions
drills.reading_name: An Overview of Private Wealth Management

questions.stem: Goals-based investing for private clients is most likely to:

options.A: pool all client wealth in one portfolio optimized against a single utility function.
options.B: allocate client wealth into sub-portfolios matched to specific goals.
options.C: assign the same risk tolerance to every goal.

rationales.A: A single portfolio optimized against one aggregate utility function is the mean-variance approach that goals-based investing departs from. Goals-based investing deliberately subdivides wealth so each goal can be funded with assets matched to its own horizon and risk tolerance rather than to an averaged objective.
rationales.B: Goals-based investing allocates client wealth into separate portfolios or sub-portfolios matched to specific goals: essential needs funded for safety, lifestyle goals at moderate risk, and aspirational goals at higher risk. Each goal carries its own return objective, risk tolerance and time horizon, which makes the structure an alternative to the single-portfolio mean-variance approach. Its practical advantage is behavioural: clients grasp risk-taking far better goal by goal than as one aggregate volatility number, so they are likelier to stay with the plan.
rationales.C: Applying one risk tolerance to every goal defeats the framework. The point of the structure is that essential needs are funded safely while aspirational goals take more risk; a uniform risk tolerance collapses the sub-portfolios back into a single aggregate allocation and leaves essential needs exposed to volatility they cannot tolerate.

questions.stem: Asset location in a private client's portfolio is most likely to:

options.A: place every asset type in the same account type for administrative simplicity.
options.B: select the geographic markets in which to invest.
options.C: assign tax-inefficient assets to tax-deferred accounts.

rationales.A: Holding every asset type in one account type for administrative simplicity forgoes the entire benefit. Tax efficiency, not simplicity, drives placement: high-turnover strategies and taxable bonds throw off ordinary income every year and belong in tax-advantaged accounts, while assets that generate little current tax can sit in a taxable account.
rationales.B: Choosing between domestic and international exposures is the asset allocation decision. Location in this context means the type of account an asset is held in — taxable, tax-deferred or Roth — not geography.
rationales.C: Asset location assigns different asset types to different account types for tax efficiency. Tax-inefficient assets — high-turnover strategies, taxable bonds, REITs producing ordinary income — go in tax-deferred accounts such as a 401(k) or IRA, where the annual tax drag disappears. Tax-efficient assets — broad-market equity ETFs, municipal bonds, buy-and-hold equity — go in taxable accounts, where low turnover and favourable rates cost little. Roth accounts hold the highest-growth assets so the compounding is permanently tax-free. Applied well, this adds materially to after-tax return without changing the asset allocation at all.

questions.stem: The taxable equivalent yield of a municipal bond is most likely calculated as:

options.A: The taxable bond yield divided by one minus the marginal tax rate.
options.B: The municipal bond yield multiplied by one minus the marginal tax rate.
options.C: The municipal bond yield divided by one minus the marginal tax rate.

rationales.A: This applies the formula to a yield that is already fully taxable, so the grossed-up figure is comparable to nothing. The taxable equivalent yield exists to gross up the tax-exempt municipal yield so it can be set beside a taxable yield on the same footing.
rationales.B: Multiplying by (1 − marginal tax rate) converts a taxable yield into an after-tax yield; it is the wrong direction here. Applied to a yield that is already tax-exempt it understates it — a 3% municipal bond would appear to yield 1.95% for an investor at a 35% rate — whereas the taxable-equivalent calculation requires dividing.
rationales.C: Taxable equivalent yield = municipal bond yield / (1 − marginal tax rate). It states the pre-tax yield a taxable bond would have to offer to leave the investor as well off as the tax-exempt municipal bond, allowing the two to be compared on an equivalent basis. For a municipal bond yielding 3% held by an investor at a 35% marginal rate: TEY = 3% / (1 − 0.35) = 3% / 0.65 = 4.62%. Compare that with a 10-year Treasury or a corporate of similar credit quality and duration to judge whether the municipal bond is attractive; the higher the investor's marginal rate, the more the grossed-up yield favours the municipal bond.

questions.stem: The after-tax return on a taxable portfolio is most likely calculated as:

options.A: The pre-tax return divided by one minus the effective tax rate.
options.B: The pre-tax return multiplied by one minus the effective tax rate.
options.C: The pre-tax return less the inflation rate.

rationales.A: Dividing grosses a return up rather than reducing it for taxes; that is the taxable-equivalent-yield construction, used to put a tax-exempt yield on a pre-tax footing. Taxes reduce a taxable return, so the adjustment has to scale it down, not up.
rationales.B: After-tax return = pre-tax return × (1 − effective tax rate on that return type), applied separately by type of return. Income — dividends and interest — is multiplied by (1 − ordinary rate); long-term capital gains are multiplied by (1 − long-term capital gains rate). For a mixed portfolio, weight the components by their share of the return. Tax-exempt income is added back untaxed, and taxes paid on distributions and on turnover are subtracted.
rationales.C: Subtracting inflation produces a real return, not an after-tax return. The two adjustments are independent: the after-tax calculation nets out taxes by income type, and the real-return calculation then removes the loss of purchasing power. A portfolio often needs both, in that order.

questions.stem: A portfolio returns 2% in dividends taxed at 35% and 6% in long-term capital gains taxed at 20%. The after-tax return is closest to:

rationales.A: 8.00% is the pre-tax total, 2% of dividends plus 6% of gains, with no tax taken off either component.
rationales.B: This applies the 35% dividend rate to the entire return: 8% × (1 − 0.35) = 5.20%. Only the 2% of dividend income is taxed at 35%; charging the ordinary rate against the capital gain component rather than 20% overstates the tax by 0.9 percentage points.
rationales.C: Tax each component at its own rate and add. Dividends after tax: 2% × (1 − 0.35) = 1.30%. Long-term capital gains after tax: 6% × (1 − 0.20) = 4.80%. Total after-tax return: 1.30% + 4.80% = 6.10%. The after-tax return is component-weighted by the respective tax rates, which is why shifting return from income into long-term gains raises the after-tax result even when the pre-tax return is unchanged.

questions.stem: A portfolio's nominal return is 8% and inflation is 3%. Using the Fisher relation, the real return is closest to:

rationales.A: This compounds the nominal return and inflation, (1.08)(1.03) − 1, instead of dividing. The answer comes out above the nominal return itself, which no positive rate of inflation can produce.
rationales.B: The Fisher relation is (1 + real) = (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation), so real = (1 + nominal)/(1 + inflation) − 1 = (1.08/1.03) − 1 = 4.85%. The familiar shortcut, real ≈ nominal − inflation, gives 8% − 3% = 5.0% and is adequate for small numbers, but it overstates the true real return, and the gap widens as inflation rises.
rationales.C: 5.00% is the simple approximation, nominal minus inflation. It overstates the real return the Fisher relation gives, 4.85%, because it omits the division by (1 + inflation); the error grows with the rate of inflation.

questions.stem: A client's strategic asset allocation is implemented across taxable, tax-deferred, and Roth accounts. Rebalancing that portfolio is most likely:

options.A: impossible across account boundaries.
options.B: indifferent to account type.
options.C: directed first to the tax-deferred accounts.

rationales.A: Account boundaries do not prevent rebalancing. A sale inside a tax-deferred account triggers no capital gains tax, so the trades needed to restore the aggregate allocation can be placed there, with loss harvesting reserved for the taxable accounts. The multi-account structure shapes where the trades are placed, not whether the portfolio can be rebalanced at all.
rationales.B: Account tax treatment changes the optimal execution path, so trades do not execute identically wherever the assets sit. The same sale that is costless in a tax-deferred account can realize a large gain in a taxable account, which is why the rebalancing trade is routed by account rather than spread evenly across accounts.
rationales.C: With multiple account types — taxable, tax-deferred, and Roth — rebalancing considers: (1) no capital gains tax impact from selling inside tax-deferred accounts, which favors rebalancing there; (2) a large gain impact in taxable accounts, where losses are harvested to offset realized gains; (3) differing asset locations, which may skew the direction in which the portfolio is rebalanced; and (4) Roth accounts, which grow tax free and are generally left to compound. Strategic multi-account rebalancing of this kind can add basis points annually to after-tax returns.

questions.stem: A comprehensive periodic performance report to a private wealth client is most likely to include:

options.A: the adviser's market forecasts in place of realized results.
options.B: after-tax, after-fee returns and progress against each stated goal.
options.C: the pre-tax, pre-fee headline return only.

rationales.A: Reporting communicates realized performance and progress toward the client's goals. Forward-looking forecasts belong to the planning and review discussion and cannot be substituted for the actual outcomes achieved over the reporting period, which is what the report exists to convey.
rationales.B: Reporting to a private client covers: total portfolio value and the change over the period; performance by portfolio segment and against the relevant benchmarks; attribution between asset allocation and security selection; after-tax and after-fee returns; progress toward the stated objectives; risk metrics such as drawdown and volatility; real return net of inflation; and cost reporting covering fees, taxes, custody, and transaction costs. Reporting frequency is typically quarterly, with an annual review of the plan itself.
rationales.C: A single gross return omits the after-tax and after-fee result the client actually keeps, and it says nothing about goal progress, risk, or attribution between allocation and selection — all of which the report should convey.

questions.stem: A private wealth adviser's behavioral role in the client relationship is most likely to:

options.A: accommodate the client's wish to sell in a drawdown.
options.B: add value through security selection alone.
options.C: discourage panic selling and performance chasing.

rationales.A: Accommodating panic selling is precisely the behavior coaching exists to prevent. Selling into a drawdown locks in the loss and takes the client out of the recovery, which is how the behavior gap destroys long-term returns; the adviser's role is to hold the client to the investment policy statement through the cycle rather than to execute the emotion.
rationales.B: This discounts coaching, which is often the adviser's single highest value-add: industry research estimates that adherence to the investment policy statement through market cycles is worth 100 to 300 basis points per year relative to abandoning the strategy. Security selection is one input among several, not the whole of what the adviser contributes.
rationales.C: The adviser plays a critical behavioral coach role: preventing panic selling during drawdowns; discouraging performance chasing after strong runs; educating the client on long-term investment horizons; and framing short-term volatility in its proper context. Adherence to the investment policy statement through market cycles is estimated by industry research to add 100 to 300 basis points per year to realized returns relative to abandonment of the strategy, which makes behavioral coaching often the adviser's highest value-add.

questions.stem: In arranging and communicating compensation, a private wealth adviser is most likely to:

options.A: rely on commissions from product sales.
options.B: disclose every fee the client bears.
options.C: keep the fee schedule from the client.

rationales.A: Commission-based compensation embeds a product-sales conflict of interest, because the adviser is paid for activity and for particular products rather than for advice. Fee-only arrangements are typically preferred for that reason, and no compensation form removes the obligation to disclose all fees.
rationales.B: Adviser fees are transparent to the client. The types include: an assets-under-management fee, for example 1% of assets, usually declining at higher asset levels; a flat or retainer fee set as a fixed dollar amount; an hourly fee for planning work; and commission-based compensation from product sales, which is subject to a conflict of interest. Fee-only arrangements are typically preferred because they eliminate the product conflict, and disclosure extends to all fees the client bears, including underlying fund expenses, custodial fees, and transaction costs.
rationales.C: Transparency is the requirement, not a negotiating disadvantage. The client cannot weigh value against cost without knowing the cost, and disclosure extends to every layer of it, including embedded fund expenses, custody, and transaction costs.

questions.stem: A client's wealth is concentrated in a single, highly appreciated equity holding. The adviser's approach to diversifying it is most likely to:

options.A: stage the sale and hedge the remainder.
options.B: liquidate the whole position at once.
options.C: rule out a collar as a hedge.

rationales.A: For clients with concentrated holdings — large employer stock, a founder position, an inherited stake — the diversification strategies available include: an outright sale, subject to its tax cost; staged liquidation over several years; exchange funds that pool the position with other concentrated holders; collars or protective puts to hedge the downside; charitable giving of appreciated shares, which is tax efficient; and borrowing against the holding to raise liquidity without a sale. Which approach fits depends on tax, control, and liquidity constraints, and the tax cost of diversifying must always be weighed against the concentration risk being carried.
rationales.B: Immediate full liquidation ignores the tax bill, any lock-up or affiliate restrictions on the shares, and the client's attachment to the holding. Staged sales, hedges, exchange funds, and charitable transfers usually dominate a single forced sale.
rationales.C: A properly structured collar hedges the downside without a sale and does not by itself trigger capital gain recognition on the underlying shares, though tax rules limit how tight the hedge may be before it is deemed a constructive sale. The collar therefore stays on the menu rather than being ruled out.

questions.stem: For a private client, the relationship between portfolio construction and estate planning is most likely:

options.A: kept strictly separate.
options.B: limited to document drafting.
options.C: integrated through asset location and basis management.

rationales.A: The two integrate rather than standing apart. Asset titling, basis management, and beneficiary designations each sit in both the portfolio decision and the estate plan, so separating the mandates forgoes the coordination that makes a transfer efficient.
rationales.B: The step-up in basis at death bears directly on which assets are held where and on when they are sold: the most-appreciated taxable assets are better held than sold late in life. The estate plan therefore reaches well past document drafting into portfolio decisions themselves.
rationales.C: Portfolio construction integrates with estate planning through: the step-up in basis on death for taxable assets, which argues for holding the most-appreciated assets in the taxable account so the basis resets; beneficiary designations on tax-deferred accounts, which drive the tax outcome for heirs; lifetime gifting using annual exclusions and the lifetime exemption; trusts, including bypass, grantor retained annuity, and generation-skipping structures; and charitable strategies such as private foundations, donor-advised funds, and charitable remainder unitrusts. Portfolio and estate decisions are coordinated so as to maximize the wealth ultimately transferred.

questions.stem: A retiree holds taxable, tax-deferred, and Roth accounts. Under a tax-efficient withdrawal sequence, the account drawn down first is most likely the:

options.A: Roth account.
options.B: tax-deferred account.
options.C: taxable account.

rationales.A: Spending the Roth first sacrifices its longest stretch of tax-free compounding, which is the whole advantage of the account. The Roth is generally drawn last, not first, so that the tax-free growth runs for as many years as possible.
rationales.B: Draining the tax-deferred account first realizes ordinary income too early and wastes the low-bracket years. Taxable accounts are typically spent first, with the tax-deferred account drawn next so that required minimum distributions do not later push income into higher brackets.
rationales.C: The tax-efficient withdrawal sequence typically runs: taxable accounts first, since the principal has already been taxed, gains are realized at the lower long-term capital gains rate, and step-up planning applies to what remains; tax-deferred accounts such as a 401(k) or IRA next, which keeps required minimum distributions from pushing income into higher brackets; and the Roth last, so that it grows tax free for the longest period. The actual sequence depends on bracket management, required minimum distributions, and healthcare planning, and some clients benefit from Roth conversions in low-income years.

questions.stem: A municipal bond yields 2.8%. For an investor whose combined federal and state marginal tax rate is 37%, the taxable-equivalent yield of that bond is closest to:

rationales.A: 1.76% is the after-tax figure, not the taxable-equivalent yield: it applies 2.8% × (1 − 0.37) and so taxes a coupon that is already tax exempt. The taxable-equivalent yield divides by (1 − t) to gross the exempt yield up, rather than multiplying by it.
rationales.B: TEY = 2.8% / (1 − 0.37) = 2.8% / 0.63 = 4.44%. The investor compares the 2.8% municipal yield with any taxable bond yielding less than 4.44%: if a Treasury yields 4.10%, the municipal bond provides the higher after-tax return. The calculation isolates the yield a taxable bond must offer to match the exempt coupon at this investor's marginal rate.
rationales.C: 2.80% is the municipal bond's own stated yield, so it ignores the tax gross-up entirely and gives no basis on which to compare a taxable alternative.

questions.stem: A portfolio's return comprises 30% dividends taxed at 35%, 60% long-term gains taxed at 20%, and 10% short-term gains taxed at 37%. The blended effective tax rate on the portfolio return is most likely:

options.A: the weighted average of the component rates.
options.B: the highest of the component rates.
options.C: not computable from the component rates.

rationales.A: The blended effective rate is the return-share weighted average of the component rates: 0.30 × 0.35 + 0.60 × 0.20 + 0.10 × 0.37 = 0.105 + 0.120 + 0.037 = 0.262, or 26.2%. The after-tax return then follows as pre-tax × (1 − 0.262) = pre-tax × 0.738. The same weighted-average approach applies to any portfolio whose return splits across dividend, long-term gain, and short-term gain treatment.
rationales.B: Weighting governs, not the maximum. The 37% short-term rate reaches only 10% of the return, while 60% is taxed at the 20% long-term rate and 30% at the 35% dividend rate, blending to 26.2% — well below the highest component rate. Applying 37% uniformly would overstate the tax drag at every horizon and in every asset class.
rationales.C: The component rates do not interact: each slice of return is taxed at its own rate, so the effective rate is a straightforward weighted average of component rates by return share — 26.2% for this composition.

questions.stem: Reporting on a portfolio managed under a goals-based approach is most likely to show:

options.A: each goal's value against its own target.
options.B: the aggregate portfolio return alone.
options.C: every goal against one common market benchmark.

rationales.A: Goals-based reporting shows: each goal's portfolio value against its target; the probability of achieving each goal from the current position; return measured against each goal-specific benchmark; and shortfall analysis where a goal is underfunded. The client can see which goals are on track and which are at risk, which enables prioritization and makes the tradeoffs between goals explicit. An aggregate view supplements the goal-level view but does not replace it.
rationales.B: An aggregate-only view defeats the purpose of goals-based investing, which is to report the funding status of each goal separately. A satisfactory total return can conceal one goal that is badly underfunded while another is overfunded.
rationales.C: Goals-based investing sets a goal-specific benchmark for each objective, built from that goal's horizon, required return, and risk tolerance. A single shared market index across all goals cannot indicate whether any particular goal is on track.

questions.stem: A portfolio earns a nominal return of 7.2% over a year in which inflation is 3.5%. The portfolio's exact real return is closest to:

rationales.A: This adds inflation to the nominal return instead of removing it: 7.2% + 3.5% = 10.7%. Inflation erodes purchasing power, so it must be divided out of the nominal return (or at most subtracted from it), never added to it.
rationales.B: The exact real return uses the Fisher relation: (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) − 1 = (1.072 / 1.035) − 1 = 1.0357 − 1 = 3.57%. The additive approximation, 7.2% − 3.5% = 3.7%, overstates the true real return because it ignores the cross-product term between the real return and inflation. That error widens as inflation rises, so the exact approach matters most in high-inflation settings and over long client horizons, where compounding the overstatement materially misstates the purchasing power the portfolio can support.
rationales.C: 3.70% is the additive approximation, 7.2% − 3.5% = 3.7%, not the exact real return. It overstates purchasing-power growth because it omits the division by (1 + inflation); the exact Fisher calculation gives (1.072 / 1.035) − 1 = 3.57%.

questions.stem: A client's portfolio has drifted from its target allocation and holds the same asset classes in both taxable and tax-deferred accounts. Rebalancing is most appropriately accomplished by:

options.A: trading equally across both account types.
options.B: trading preferentially in the taxable accounts.
options.C: trading preferentially in the tax-deferred accounts.

rationales.A: Trading equally across account types ignores where each asset is held and therefore the tax consequence of each trade. Tax-aware rebalancing routes transactions to the accounts in which they trigger the least tax, so treating taxable and tax-deferred accounts identically needlessly realizes capital gains.
rationales.B: Rebalancing inside a taxable account realizes capital gains that could have been avoided, and resetting cost basis is not a benefit that offsets the tax paid today. Because trades inside a tax-deferred account generate no current capital gains tax, those accounts are the preferred venue for the same trades.
rationales.C: Rebalancing trades should be directed first to tax-deferred accounts, where no capital gains tax is triggered. Where a taxable account must be traded, harvest losses to offset realized gains; use new cash flows (savings, dividends, interest) to buy underweight assets rather than selling overweight ones; and favor tax-efficient vehicles (ETFs or direct indexing rather than commingled mutual funds) to limit forced distributions. Together these steps hold the portfolio near its target allocation while minimizing the tax drag that rebalancing would otherwise create.

questions.stem: Regarding tax-efficient charitable giving by private clients, the most appropriate statement is that:

options.A: donating long-term appreciated securities is tax-efficient.
options.B: only cash gifts are tax-efficient.
options.C: the structure of a gift does not affect its tax treatment.

rationales.A: Donating securities held long-term that have appreciated is the core tax-efficient gift: the client avoids the capital gains tax a sale would have triggered and may deduct the full fair market value. Related structures extend the same idea. Donor-advised funds let a client bunch contributions into a high-income year for a larger itemized deduction and then grant the money out over time; qualified charitable distributions from an IRA (from age 70½, up to the annual limit) satisfy giving out of pre-tax assets; charitable remainder trusts pay income to the client with the remainder passing to charity; and private foundations suit large-scale, multi-year giving. Which structure fits depends on the scale of the gift and the client's goals.
rationales.B: Cash is often the least tax-efficient gift. Donating appreciated long-term securities both avoids the capital gains tax on the embedded appreciation and allows a deduction at fair market value, so a securities gift does not forfeit the charitable deduction.
rationales.C: Charitable structures are among the most powerful tax-planning tools available to private clients, so how a gift is made matters: the form of the gift changes both the deduction claimed and the treatment of embedded capital gains. Donor-advised funds, qualified charitable distributions, charitable remainder trusts and private foundations each alter the timing and the character of the tax benefit.

questions.stem: Regarding a Roth conversion undertaken by a private client, the most appropriate statement is that it:

options.A: is advantageous regardless of current and future tax rates.
options.B: moves pre-tax IRA assets into a Roth account.
options.C: moves Roth assets back into a pre-tax IRA.

rationales.A: A conversion is favorable only in particular circumstances, not universally. It pays tax now in exchange for tax-free growth later, so it helps when the current tax rate is below the expected future rate and destroys value when the reverse holds.
rationales.B: A Roth conversion moves pre-tax IRA assets into a Roth account, paying tax on the converted amount now in exchange for tax-free growth and tax-free withdrawals later. It is favorable when the current tax rate is lower than the expected future rate; in low-income years such as early retirement before required minimum distributions begin, or a sabbatical; when the conversion tax can be paid from taxable assets rather than from the IRA itself, which preserves the full balance inside the Roth; and when the horizon is long enough for tax-free compounding to matter. It is unfavorable when those conditions reverse, which is why conversions are planned across several years alongside income and required-distribution projections rather than decided in isolation.
rationales.C: This reverses the direction of the transaction. A Roth conversion moves pre-tax IRA assets into a Roth, paying tax now in exchange for tax-free growth; it does not move Roth assets back into a pre-tax IRA to defer current taxes.

drills.los_text: discuss the differences between private and institutional clients and formulate an appropriate Investment Policy Statement for private clients
drills.reading_name: An Overview of Private Wealth Management

questions.stem: Compared with those of institutional investors, the investment horizons of private clients are most likely:

options.A: longer and less variable.
options.B: perpetual, given multi-generational wealth transfer.
options.C: finite and driven by the life cycle.

rationales.A: This reverses the relationship. Endowments and sovereign wealth funds are typically perpetual, and defined benefit pension horizons run with member demographics, so institutional horizons are generally the longer and more stable ones; private-client horizons are the shorter and more variable.
rationales.B: A multi-generational orientation in some high-net-worth families is not a truly perpetual horizon. Individual goals still resolve at datable points — retirement, education funding, mortality — so the horizon remains finite and life-cycle-driven even where wealth is intended to pass to heirs.
rationales.C: Private-client horizons are finite and driven by the life cycle: earning years, retirement and mortality set the dates by which goals must be funded. Endowments and sovereign wealth funds often have perpetual horizons, and defined benefit pension horizons are tied to member demographics. Because health, career and family events shift the client's goal dates, private-client horizons are both shorter and more variable than most institutional horizons, which is why private portfolios are managed around approaching goal dates rather than around a permanent spending rule.

questions.stem: Compared with those of institutional investors, the tax situations of private clients are most likely:

options.A: simpler, with all income taxed at one marginal rate.
options.B: narrower, confined to income tax alone.
options.C: more complex, spanning income, estate, gift and wealth taxes.

rationales.A: Private taxation is the more complex of the two. Ordinary income versus capital gains treatment, estate and inheritance tax, gift tax, and wealth tax in some jurisdictions apply on top of one another, and holdings sit across taxable, tax-deferred and tax-exempt accounts, so income is not aggregated at a single marginal rate. Most institutions are tax-exempt or face simplified treatment.
rationales.B: Estate and inheritance, gift, and in some jurisdictions wealth taxes fall on individuals and households and are layered on top of income tax, so private tax complexity is not confined to income tax. Many institutions — endowments, pensions, foundations — are tax-exempt rather than the parties bearing these levies.
rationales.C: Private clients face complex personal tax situations: income tax with different treatment of ordinary income and capital gains, estate or inheritance tax, gift tax, wealth tax in some jurisdictions, and tax-advantaged accounts for retirement and education. Most institutional investors — endowments, pensions, foundations — are tax-exempt or have simplified tax treatment. The private-wealth adviser must therefore engineer after-tax outcomes across several account types at once, making asset location as much a decision as asset allocation.

questions.stem: Regarding the governance of investment decisions, the most appropriate statement is that:

options.A: institutional decisions are made by an individual manager without oversight.
options.B: private-client decisions are made by the individual or family.
options.C: private-client decisions are made by a formal investment committee.

rationales.A: This reverses the governance model. Institutions rely on formal structures — investment committees, a written investment policy statement and professional staff — so decisions are not made by a single manager acting without oversight.
rationales.B: For private clients, the individual or the family makes the decisions. Those decisions are influenced by emotion, behavioral biases and family dynamics, and the decision-makers often lack investment expertise. Institutional investors, by contrast, have formal governance structures — investment committees operating under a written investment policy statement — professional staff and disciplined, documented processes. The private-wealth adviser's role is to bridge that gap, supplying the structure, discipline and documentation an institution gets from its governance framework.
rationales.C: This attributes institutional governance to private clients. Formal investment committees and policy-statement-driven processes characterize institutions; private-client decisions are made informally by the individual or family, subject to emotion, bias and family dynamics.

questions.stem: The investment objectives of a private client are most likely:

options.A: confined to maximizing total wealth.
options.B: multi-dimensional and personal.
options.C: singular and impersonal, as for institutions.

rationales.A: Private-client objectives are identifiable and specific rather than a single wealth-maximization target. Retirement lifestyle, legacy for heirs, education funding, charitable giving and planned purchases are concrete, personal goals, and they frequently compete with one another for the same pool of assets.
rationales.B: Private-client objectives are typically multi-dimensional and personal: retirement lifestyle, legacy for heirs, education for children, charitable giving, specific purchase goals such as a home or a business, and funding care in later life. Institutional objectives are typically singular and quantifiable — funded status for a pension, a spending policy for an endowment. Because private goals may conflict with one another, the adviser must prioritize among them, which is why private-client planning assigns assets to individual goals instead of optimizing one aggregate objective.
rationales.C: Singularity describes institutional mandates — a pension's funded status, an endowment's spending policy. Private-client objectives are multi-dimensional and personal, covering lifestyle, legacy, education and giving goals that often conflict and must be ranked.

questions.stem: A private client's risk tolerance is most appropriately assessed as:

options.A: willingness always overriding ability.
options.B: ability alone.
options.C: ability combined with willingness.

rationales.A: Where willingness exceeds ability, ability binds: a client cannot prudently take more risk than financial capacity allows, whatever their stated comfort level. The framework reconciles the two dimensions rather than letting psychological comfort always govern the decision.
rationales.B: Ability — the financial capacity to bear losses given wealth, income stability and horizon — is only half the analysis. Behavioral willingness completes it, and ignoring willingness produces a policy the client abandons in a drawdown.
rationales.C: Private-client risk tolerance combines ability, the financial capacity to bear losses given wealth, income stability and horizon, with willingness, the behavioral and psychological comfort with loss. Willingness is often lower than ability, driven by loss aversion, recency bias or inexperience with investing, and the binding constraint is ordinarily the lower of the two. Institutional risk tolerance is typically framed relative to a liability structure or a spending policy, with far less behavioral variance to reconcile.

questions.stem: Compared with those of institutional investors, the liquidity needs of private clients are most likely:

options.A: different in size rather than in timing.
options.B: irregular and unpredictable in timing.
options.C: more predictable, allowing smaller reserves.

rationales.A: The difference lies in timing as well as size. Institutional outflows — pension benefit payments, endowment spending rules — are comparatively regular and forecastable, while private needs are lumpy and personal, so one common reserve policy will not serve both. Private portfolios carry proportionally larger cash reserves precisely because the timing is unpredictable.
rationales.B: Private clients have irregular, unpredictable liquidity needs: tuition, home purchases, medical events, family emergencies and tax payments. Institutional investors typically have regular, predictable needs — pension benefit payments, endowment spending rules — that can be budgeted years ahead. The private-wealth adviser therefore maintains higher cash and near-cash reserves, since an unplanned call on the portfolio would otherwise force the sale of illiquid or depressed assets at the worst possible moment.
rationales.C: Household budgets are not fixed in the relevant sense. Tuition, home purchases, medical events and emergencies arrive irregularly and unpredictably, so private liquidity needs are less predictable than institutional ones and private reserves must be larger, not smaller.

questions.stem: An adviser serving private clients, rather than institutional ones, is most likely subject to:

options.A: suitability or fiduciary standards.
options.B: no regime, as individual accounts are unregulated.
options.C: the prudent investor rule and ERISA.

rationales.A: A private-client adviser works under a suitability standard or, in many jurisdictions, a fiduciary one, together with know-your-client and anti-money-laundering compliance and cross-border reporting where the client, the family, or the assets span more than one jurisdiction. The institutional side is governed differently: the prudent investor rule, ERISA for US pension plans, and regulations specialized by institution type for foundations, endowments, and insurance companies. The private wealth adviser therefore has to navigate the client's own regulatory context, and in family-office structures coordinate requirements across several jurisdictions at once. Regulatory frameworks differ by both client type and jurisdiction.
rationales.B: Individual accounts are not outside regulation. The adviser still owes suitability or fiduciary duties, must complete know-your-client and anti-money-laundering checks, and faces cross-border reporting obligations when the client holds assets or residence in more than one jurisdiction. Treating the private-client relationship as unregulated is the error here.
